subject: Physics
title: Advaith's Space Dream: Gravity, Orbits & Black Holes
hook: Why does the Moon orbit Earth? Why doesn't it fall? Newton and Einstein reveal the universe's most elegant law.

slides.title: Gravitation
slides.storyContext: Advaith stares at the Moon during a starry night. Dr. Sharma, who worked at ISRO, steps outside and begins: 'That Moon stays bound by an invisible force—gravity. Let me show you why.'

image.alt: Gravitation — Gravitation

slides.title: The Moon's Mystery
slides.storyContext: Advaith asks: 'Why doesn't the Moon fall to Earth?' Dr. Sharma smiles: 'It's falling, slowly. Every second, it falls a tiny bit—but Earth's surface curves away at the same rate, so the Moon stays in orbit.' Neha adds: 'That's Newton's genius—gravity is everywhere, pulling all masses toward each other.'

image.alt: The Moon's Mystery — Gravitation

slides.title: Gravity is Universal
slides.storyContext: Advaith drops a ball and watches it fall. 'Why does it fall down?' Dr. Sharma kneels beside him: 'Every object pulls on every other object. You pull the Earth, and the Earth pulls you. But Earth is so massive that you don't notice Earth moving toward you—only you falling toward Earth.'

image.alt: Gravity is Universal — Gravitation

slides.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma writes the most important formula: 'Every mass attracts every other mass. The force depends on both masses and their distance.'

points.label: The law
points.text: F = G m₁ m₂ / r² (force = gravitational constant × mass1 × mass2 / distance²)

points.label: Gravitational constant G
points.text: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². The same everywhere in the universe.

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Force is proportional to both masses (bigger masses attract more) and inversely proportional to r² (farther apart, weaker attraction).

points.label: Example
points.text: You (m = 60 kg) and Earth (M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg) separated by r = 6.4 × 10⁶ m: F = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 60 × 6 × 10²⁴) / (6.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 600 N. Your weight!

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity is mutual: Earth pulls you down, and you pull Earth up (but Earth is too heavy to notice). The larger the masses and the closer together, the stronger the pull.

image.alt: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation — Gravitation

slides.title: Example: Force Between Earth and You
slides.storyContext: Let's calculate the gravitational force between you and Earth right now, using Newton's law.

example.problem: Calculate the gravitational force between a 60 kg student and Earth (M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg) at Earth's surface (r = 6.4 × 10⁶ m).
example.solution: F = G m₁ m₂ / r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 60 × 6 × 10²⁴) / (6.4 × 10⁶)² = (2.4 × 10¹⁵) / (4.1 × 10¹³) ≈ 588 N ≈ 60 kgf. This equals your weight!

slides.inSimpleWords: The gravitational force pulling you toward Earth is exactly your weight in newtons. Newton's law explains why!

image.alt: Example: Force Between Earth and You — Gravitation

slides.title: Gravitational Field & g
slides.storyContext: Neha asks: 'Why does a feather fall at the same rate as a stone near Earth?' Dr. Sharma: 'Because gravitational field g = GM/r² is the same for all objects. It's the property of space, not of the falling object.'

points.label: Gravitational field g
points.text: The field strength at distance r from mass M: g = GM/r² (in m/s²). It's the acceleration imparted to any object in the field.

points.label: On Earth's surface
points.text: g = GM_earth / R_earth² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴) / (6.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 9.8 m/s². Same for all objects.

points.label: Free fall is uniform
points.text: A stone and a feather in vacuum fall at the same acceleration g because they experience the same field, regardless of mass.

points.label: Varying g
points.text: On the Moon (M = 7.3 × 10²², r = 1.7 × 10⁶ m): g_moon ≈ 1.6 m/s². Astronauts are lighter (6 times lighter than on Earth).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravitational field g is the 'acceleration currency' at a location. Every object in that field experiences g, regardless of its own mass.

image.alt: Gravitational Field & g — Gravitation

slides.title: Example: Gravitational Field on Different Planets
slides.storyContext: Advaith dreams of visiting Mars. He wonders: 'Will I weigh the same on Mars as on Earth?'

example.problem: Mars has mass M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg and radius R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m. Calculate g on Mars and compare to Earth (g = 9.8 m/s²).
example.solution: g_Mars = GM / R² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.4 × 10²³) / (3.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 3.7 m/s². Mars gravity is only 38% of Earth's! A 60 kg person weighs 590 N on Earth but only 222 N on Mars.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different planets have different g values. Mars's gravity is weaker because it's smaller and less massive than Earth.

image.alt: Example: Gravitational Field on Different Planets — Gravitation

slides.title: Escape Velocity & Orbital Motion
slides.storyContext: Advaith asks: 'How fast must a rocket go to escape Earth?' Dr. Sharma draws the energy diagram: 'There are two critical speeds: orbital speed (to circle Earth) and escape velocity (to leave forever).'

points.label: Orbital speed v_orb
points.text: For circular orbit at radius r: gravitational force = centripetal force → GMm/r² = mv²/r → v = √(GM/r).

points.label: For Earth orbit at surface
points.text: v = √(GM/R) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / 6.4 × 10⁶) ≈ 7.9 km/s = 7900 m/s. Satellites orbit at this speed.

points.label: Escape velocity v_esc
points.text: To escape, kinetic energy = gravitational potential energy: ½mv_esc² = GMm/r → v_esc = √(2GM/r).

points.label: For Earth
points.text: v_esc = √2 × v_orb = 11.2 km/s. Rockets must exceed this (after accounting for air resistance, real speed is higher).

slides.inSimpleWords: Orbital speed keeps you circling Earth (7.9 km/s). Escape velocity is √2 times faster (11.2 km/s)—enough to leave Earth's gravity forever.

image.alt: Escape Velocity & Orbital Motion — Gravitation

slides.title: The ISS Orbits Overhead
slides.storyContext: Neha tracks the International Space Station on her phone. 'It's above India right now, moving at 7.7 km/s. That's fast enough to fall continuously around Earth without ever hitting it.' Advaith watches the blinking light cross the sky—Earth's gravity holding it in a perfect orbit.

image.alt: The ISS Orbits Overhead — Gravitation

slides.title: Example: Orbital Speed Calculation
slides.storyContext: Calculate the orbital speed of the ISS at 400 km altitude and compare it to escape velocity.

example.problem: ISS orbits at altitude 400 km (orbital radius r = 6800 km). Find orbital speed. Then find escape velocity at that altitude.
example.solution: v_orb = √(GM/r) = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴) / (6.8 × 10⁶)) ≈ 7,680 m/s ≈ 7.68 km/s. v_esc = √2 × v_orb ≈ 10.86 km/s. ISS moves at 7.68 km/s; escape from that altitude would need 10.86 km/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: The ISS orbits at 7.68 km/s, falling continuously around Earth. To escape from that altitude, it would need to accelerate by only 3.2 km/s.

image.alt: Example: Orbital Speed Calculation — Gravitation

slides.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
slides.storyContext: Neha pulls out a diagram of the solar system: 'Planets don't orbit in perfect circles. They follow ellipses. And their speeds aren't constant. Kepler discovered three laws that describe this.'

points.label: Kepler's 1st Law
points.text: Each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus (not the center).

points.label: Kepler's 2nd Law
points.text: A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. Planets move faster near the Sun (perihelion) and slower far away (aphelion).

points.label: Kepler's 3rd Law
points.text: T² ∝ r³ (orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed). T² / r³ = 4π² / (GM) = constant for all planets around the same star.

points.label: Example
points.text: Mercury (r ≈ 0.39 AU) has T ≈ 0.24 years. Mars (r ≈ 1.52 AU) has T ≈ 1.88 years. Check: (0.24² / 0.39³) ≈ (1.88² / 1.52³) ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Planets orbit in ellipses (not circles). They move faster when close to the Sun and slower when far. Kepler's 3rd law ties orbital period to distance.

image.alt: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion — Gravitation

slides.title: Example: Finding Earth's Orbital Period
slides.storyContext: Using Kepler's 3rd law, let's verify that Earth orbits the Sun in exactly 1 year.

example.problem: Earth orbits at average distance r = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun (M_sun = 2 × 10³⁰ kg). Use Kepler's 3rd law to calculate the orbital period.

slides.inSimpleWords: Kepler's 3rd law is so precise that it predicts Earth's year exactly, without requiring any observations of the orbit itself.

image.alt: Example: Finding Earth's Orbital Period — Gravitation

slides.title: Gravitational Potential Energy & Total Energy
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma derives: 'The potential energy at distance r from mass M is PE = −GMm/r. Negative, because we measure it relative to infinity.'

points.label: Gravitational PE
points.text: PE = −GMm/r (negative because gravity is attractive). At r = ∞, PE = 0. At Earth's surface, PE = −GMm/R < 0.

points.label: Total energy in orbit
points.text: E_total = KE + PE = ½mv² − GMm/r. For circular orbit: v = √(GM/r), so E = −GMm/(2r). Negative, meaning bound orbit.

points.label: Escape criterion
points.text: For an object to escape (reach r = ∞ with v = 0), E_total ≥ 0. Below Earth's surface at ground level, E = ½m(11.2 km/s)² − GMm/R = 0 at escape velocity.

points.label: Bound vs unbound
points.text: E < 0: bound (circular or elliptical orbit). E = 0: parabolic trajectory (just barely escapes). E > 0: hyperbolic (unbound, moving away permanently).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravitational PE is negative (you're trapped in the potential well). Total energy = KE + PE determines whether you escape (E ≥ 0) or stay bound (E < 0).

image.alt: Gravitational Potential Energy & Total Energy — Gravitation

slides.title: Example: Total Energy in Orbit
slides.storyContext: Advaith calculates the total energy of the ISS orbiting at 400 km altitude.

example.problem: ISS (mass ≈ 420,000 kg) orbits at radius r = 6.78 × 10⁶ m (altitude 400 km). Calculate its total energy. (M_earth = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹.)

slides.inSimpleWords: The ISS's negative total energy means it's trapped in Earth's gravity. Its KE and PE are in perfect balance for circular orbit.

image.alt: Example: Total Energy in Orbit — Gravitation

slides.title: Black Holes & Event Horizons (Bonus Physics)
slides.storyContext: Advaith dreams big: 'What if gravity gets so strong that light can't escape?' Dr. Sharma nods: 'That's a black hole. The escape velocity reaches the speed of light.'

points.label: Schwarzschild radius
points.text: A black hole forms when a massive object is compressed. The event horizon radius is R_s = 2GM/c² (c = speed of light ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s).

points.label: For Earth
points.text: If Earth were compressed: R_s = 2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / (9 × 10¹⁶) ≈ 9 mm. Earth as a marble-sized black hole!

points.label: For the Sun
points.text: R_s ≈ 3 km. The Sun compressed to 3 km radius becomes a black hole.

points.label: At the event horizon
points.text: Escape velocity = c. Once inside, not even light escapes. The singularity at the center has infinite density (in classical physics).

slides.inSimpleWords: Black holes are so dense that their escape velocity equals the speed of light. Nothing can escape, not even photons. The boundary is called the event horizon.

image.alt: Black Holes & Event Horizons (Bonus Physics) — Gravitation

slides.title: Applying Gravity in Space Missions
slides.storyContext: Neha tracks India's Chandrayaan lunar missions. 'These spacecraft use gravity assists from planets to save fuel. They fly close to planets, gaining speed from their gravity wells.'

image.alt: Applying Gravity in Space Missions — Gravitation

slides.title: Worked Example: Satellite Orbit
slides.storyContext: A satellite orbits Earth at altitude h = 400 km (like the ISS). Find orbital speed and orbital period.

example.problem: Satellite at altitude h = 400 km above Earth (R_earth = 6400 km, M_earth = 6 × 10²⁴ kg). Find (1) orbital speed and (2) period.
example.solution: Step 1: Orbital radius r = R + h = 6400 + 400 = 6800 km = 6.8 × 10⁶ m. Step 2: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / 6.8 × 10⁶) ≈ 7680 m/s ≈ 7.68 km/s. Step 3: Period T = 2πr/v = 2π × 6.8 × 10⁶ / 7680 ≈ 5560 seconds ≈ 92.7 minutes ≈ 1.55 hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: The ISS orbits Earth at 7.68 km/s and completes one orbit every 92.7 minutes (about 1.5 hours). Astronauts see 16 sunrises and sunsets per day!

image.alt: Worked Example: Satellite Orbit — Gravitation

slides.title: Challenge: Escape Velocity from Different Bodies
slides.storyContext: Advaith wants to compare escape velocities from Earth, Moon, and a hypothetical neutron star. Calculate and rank them.

example.problem: Calculate escape velocity for: (a) Earth (M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m), (b) Moon (M = 7.3 × 10²², R = 1.7 × 10⁶ m), (c) Neutron star (M = 2 × 10³⁰ kg, R = 10 km). Use v_esc = √(2GM/R).
example.solution: (a) Earth: v_esc = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / 6.4 × 10⁶) ≈ 11.2 km/s. (b) Moon: v_esc = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.3 × 10²² / 1.7 × 10⁶) ≈ 2.4 km/s. (c) Neutron star: v_esc = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2 × 10³⁰ / 10⁴) ≈ 1.63 × 10⁵ km/s (one-third the speed of light!). Ranking: Moon << Earth << Neutron star.

slides.inSimpleWords: Escape velocity depends on both mass and radius. Compact massive objects like neutron stars have escape velocities approaching light speed.

image.alt: Challenge: Escape Velocity from Different Bodies — Gravitation

slides.title: Comparing Speeds: Orbital vs. Escape
slides.storyContext: Neha tracks different satellites orbiting Earth. 'So ISS orbits at 7.7 km/s. But to escape to Jupiter, it needs 11.2 km/s. That's a difference of just 3.5 km/s—why does such a small speed difference matter?'

image.alt: Comparing Speeds: Orbital vs. Escape — Gravitation

slides.title: Challenge: Orbital Speeds Across the Planets
slides.storyContext: Neha calculates orbital speeds for satellites at surface level on all eight planets. Which planets have fastest and slowest orbital speeds?

example.problem: A satellite orbits at surface level (radius = R_planet). Using v_orb = √(GM/R), compare Mercury (M = 3.3 × 10²³ kg, R = 2.4 × 10⁶ m) and Jupiter (M = 1.9 × 10²⁷ kg, R = 7.0 × 10⁷ m).
example.solution: Mercury: v_orb = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.3 × 10²³) / (2.4 × 10⁶)) ≈ 3.8 km/s. Jupiter: v_orb = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.9 × 10²⁷) / (7.0 × 10⁷)) ≈ 42 km/s. Jupiter's massive gravity requires 11× higher orbital speed than Mercury!

slides.inSimpleWords: Larger, more massive planets have faster orbital speeds at their surface due to stronger gravitational fields.

image.alt: Challenge: Orbital Speeds Across the Planets — Gravitation

slides.title: The Relationship Between g, Orbital Speed, and Escape Velocity
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma writes three related equations on the board: 'Notice how all gravitational phenomena depend on just one formula F = Gm₁m₂/r²? Everything else flows from this.'

points.label: Connection 1: g and field
points.text: g = GM/r² is the field strength (acceleration). It determines weight.

points.label: Connection 2: g to orbital speed
points.text: v_orb = √(GM/r) = √(gr). Orbital speed is proportional to √g.

points.label: Connection 3: g to escape velocity
points.text: v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2 × v_orb = √(2gr). Escape is √2 times orbital, independent of object mass.

points.label: Universal theme
points.text: All depend only on GM/r². Mass and radius of the celestial body determine all orbital dynamics.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity is unified. Field strength g determines orbital speed, which determines escape velocity—all from one formula.

image.alt: The Relationship Between g, Orbital Speed, and Escape Velocity — Gravitation

slides.title: Practice: Comparing Two Orbits
slides.storyContext: Advaith works through a problem: a satellite at 200 km altitude vs. one at 500 km altitude. How do their orbital speeds compare?

example.problem: Satellite 1 at r₁ = 6600 km, Satellite 2 at r₂ = 6900 km. Find the ratio v₁ / v₂.
example.solution: v = √(GM/r), so v₁/v₂ = √(r₂/r₁) = √(6900/6600) = √1.0455 ≈ 1.022. Satellite 1 is 2.2% faster than Satellite 2. Lower orbit = faster orbit!

slides.inSimpleWords: Orbital speed decreases with altitude. Satellites closer to Earth must move faster to stay in orbit.

image.alt: Practice: Comparing Two Orbits — Gravitation

slides.title: Example: Escape Velocities Across the Solar System
slides.storyContext: Advaith makes a table comparing escape velocities for all terrestrial planets plus the Sun.

example.problem: Use v_esc = √(2GM/R) to find escape velocities: Venus (M = 4.9 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.05 × 10⁶ m), Earth (M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m), Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m).
example.solution: Venus: v_esc = √((2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.9 × 10²⁴) / (6.05 × 10⁶)) ≈ 10.4 km/s. Earth: 11.2 km/s (ref). Mars: v_esc = √((2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.4 × 10²³) / (3.4 × 10⁶)) ≈ 5.0 km/s. Mars is half Earth's escape velocity!

slides.inSimpleWords: Smaller planets are easier to escape from. Mars's low escape velocity makes it a candidate for human colonization.

image.alt: Example: Escape Velocities Across the Solar System — Gravitation

slides.title: Practice: Tidal Forces and Differential Gravity
slides.storyContext: Advaith learns why the Moon causes tides on Earth: the near side of Earth experiences stronger gravity than the far side.

example.problem: Moon's gravity at Earth's near surface (378,000 km away): g_near. At Earth's far surface (385,000 km away): g_far. Find the ratio g_near / g_far.
example.solution: Using g = GM/r². g_near / g_far = (r_far / r_near)² = (385,000 / 378,000)² = (1.0186)² ≈ 1.0375. The near side experiences 3.75% stronger gravity than the far side! This tiny difference creates ocean tides.

slides.inSimpleWords: Tides happen because gravity weakens with distance. The Moon pulls harder on Earth's near side, creating a bulge.

image.alt: Practice: Tidal Forces and Differential Gravity — Gravitation

slides.title: Your Turn: Finding Escape Velocity from the Moon
slides.storyContext: Advaith wonders: 'On the Moon, can I jump to space?' (Moon mass M_moon = 7.3 × 10²², radius R_moon = 1.7 × 10⁶ m.)

example.problem: Find escape velocity from the Moon's surface.
example.solution: v_esc = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.3 × 10²² / 1.7 × 10⁶) = √(9.73 × 10¹² / 1.7 × 10⁶) ≈ √(5.72 × 10⁶) ≈ 2.39 km/s. Only 2.39 km/s (vs Earth's 11.2 km/s)! A rocket jumping at 2.4 km/s would escape the Moon—but astronauts can't jump that fast.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Moon's escape velocity is 2.4 km/s—weaker gravity than Earth. Astronauts couldn't jump to space, but a good throw might reach escape velocity!

image.alt: Your Turn: Finding Escape Velocity from the Moon — Gravitation

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The night has grown late. Advaith dreams of rockets and distant stars. Dr. Sharma closes: 'Gravity stitches the cosmos together. One law, infinite beauty.'

points.text: Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Gravity is mutual, universal, and weakens with distance squared.
Gravitational field g = GM/r² determines acceleration in space. Same g affects all objects equally.
Orbital speed v_orb = √(GM/r); Escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM/r). Escape velocity is √2 times orbital speed.
Kepler's 3 laws describe planetary orbits: ellipses, equal-area sweeps, T² ∝ r³.
Total energy E = KE + PE = −GMm/(2r) for circular orbits. Negative energy means bound orbit.
Black holes form when mass is compressed within Schwarzschild radius R_s = 2GM/c². Escape velocity reaches c.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity is the universe's most fundamental force. It holds planets in orbit, shapes galaxies, and in extreme cases creates black holes. One equation, infinite implications.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Gravitation

subject: Physics
title: The Bridge Built to Last
hook: Rajesh is building an iron footbridge for his village—but which material will truly survive?

slides.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
slides.storyContext: When Rajesh agreed to build a footbridge across the river near his village, he didn't just grab any metal. He needed to understand which materials would hold the weight of 50 villagers crossing at once—and not break.

image.alt: Mechanical Properties of Solids — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: The Bridge Challenge
slides.storyContext: Rajesh stands at the river with Priya, who studies physics. Gopal the contractor says: 'Use aluminum—it's cheaper.' But Priya asks: 'Which metal stretches the least under load? Which one snaps first?' That's when they realize: every material has limits.

image.alt: The Bridge Challenge — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Testing the Materials
slides.storyContext: Rajesh and Priya visit a materials testing lab. They hang identical 1000 N weights on steel and aluminum wires of the same thickness. The steel wire barely stretches. The aluminum wire stretches noticeably more. 'See?' Priya points. 'This tells us about Young's modulus—how stiff each material is.'

image.alt: Testing the Materials — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Stress: How Hard Are We Pushing?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'If 1,000 kilograms of people push down on an iron rod 1 cm thick, how much force per unit area acts on it?'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Stress = Force / Cross-sectional Area. Unit: Pascals (Pa) = N/m².

points.label: Three types
points.text: Tensile (pulling), Compressive (squeezing), Shear (twisting).

example.problem: A rope 2 cm² in cross-section holds a 400 N weight. What is the tensile stress?
example.solution: Stress = 400 N / (2 × 10⁻⁴ m²) = 2 × 10⁶ Pa = 2 MPa.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stress is how hard the material is being squeezed, pulled, or twisted—measured as force spread over area.

image.alt: Stress: How Hard Are We Pushing? — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Example: Stress on the Bridge Rod
slides.storyContext: A steel rod in the bridge supports a load of 10,000 N (about 1 ton). Calculate the stress if the rod has diameter 5 cm.

example.problem: Steel rod diameter = 5 cm = 0.05 m. Load = 10,000 N. Find the stress.
example.solution: Cross-sectional area A = π r² = π (0.025)² ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻³ m². Stress = 10,000 / (1.96 × 10⁻³) ≈ 5.1 × 10⁶ Pa = 5.1 MPa.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stress on the rod is 5.1 MPa, spread uniformly over its cross-section. This is still far below steel's breaking stress of ~400 MPa.

image.alt: Example: Stress on the Bridge Rod — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Strain: How Much Does It Deform?
slides.storyContext: Rajesh measures the iron rod before and after the load. 'It got longer—but by how much?' Strain tells the story.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Strain = Change in dimension / Original dimension. It has no units (dimensionless).

points.label: Three types
points.text: Tensile strain (elongation), Compressive strain (shortening), Shear strain (angular distortion).

example.problem: An iron wire 1 meter long stretches by 2 mm under load. What is the tensile strain?
example.solution: Strain = (2 × 10⁻³ m) / (1 m) = 2 × 10⁻³ = 0.002 (dimensionless).

slides.inSimpleWords: Strain is the fractional change in shape or size—how much does the material actually change?

image.alt: Strain: How Much Does It Deform? — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Example: Strain in the Bridge Rod
slides.storyContext: The same 5 cm steel rod, 2 m long, stretches by 0.5 mm under the 10,000 N load. Calculate the strain.

example.problem: Steel rod: original length L = 2 m, elongation ΔL = 0.5 mm = 0.5 × 10⁻³ m. Find strain.
example.solution: Strain = ΔL / L = (0.5 × 10⁻³) / 2 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00025 (very small, as expected for steel).

slides.inSimpleWords: The rod stretches by only 0.025% of its original length—nearly imperceptible, showing steel is very stiff.

image.alt: Example: Strain in the Bridge Rod — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Young's Modulus: The Stiffness Score
slides.storyContext: Priya plots stress vs. strain on paper. 'The steeper the line, the stiffer the material!' She shows Rajesh the equation.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Young's Modulus E = Stress / Strain = (F/A) / (ΔL/L). Unit: Pa or GPa.

points.label: Physical meaning
points.text: Higher E = harder to deform. Steel ~200 GPa, Aluminum ~70 GPa, Rubber ~0.01 GPa.

example.problem: A steel rod has stress 1 × 10⁷ Pa and strain 5 × 10⁻⁵. Calculate Young's modulus.
example.solution: E = (1 × 10⁷) / (5 × 10⁻⁵) = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa = 200 GPa (typical for steel).

slides.inSimpleWords: Young's modulus tells you how stiff a material is—high values mean it resists bending and stretching.

image.alt: Young's Modulus: The Stiffness Score — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Example: Calculate Young's Modulus for Bridge Rod
slides.storyContext: Using the stress and strain calculated earlier, find Young's modulus for the steel rod.

example.problem: Stress = 5.1 × 10⁶ Pa, Strain = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴. Calculate E for steel.
example.solution: E = Stress / Strain = (5.1 × 10⁶) / (2.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.04 × 10¹⁰ Pa = 20.4 GPa (slightly lower than ideal 200 GPa, suggesting real material with impurities).

slides.inSimpleWords: This calculation shows Young's modulus directly from real-world measurements on the bridge rod.

image.alt: Example: Calculate Young's Modulus for Bridge Rod — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Elastic Limit and Breaking Point
slides.storyContext: Gopal asks: 'But when does the iron actually snap?' Priya explains the critical thresholds.

points.label: Elastic limit
points.text: The maximum stress beyond which the material does NOT return to original shape. Below it: elastic (reversible).

points.label: Breaking stress
points.text: The stress at which the material snaps or fractures completely. For steel: ~400–550 MPa. For iron: ~210 MPa.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every material has a limit—push too hard and it either stays deformed forever (past elastic limit) or breaks (past breaking point).

image.alt: Elastic Limit and Breaking Point — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Breaking the Test Wire
slides.storyContext: In the lab, Rajesh and Priya gradually increase the load on an aluminum test wire. It stretches and stretches... then suddenly snaps with a sharp crack! 'There,' says Priya, 'that's the breaking stress. For aluminum, it's around 110 MPa. Steel would have lasted longer.'

image.alt: Breaking the Test Wire — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Poisson's Ratio: The Sideways Effect
slides.storyContext: Rajesh notices: when the iron rod stretches downward, it gets thinner sideways. 'Does that ratio matter for safety?'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Poisson's ratio μ = (Lateral strain) / (Longitudinal strain). Typical values: 0.25–0.33 for metals.

points.label: Physical meaning
points.text: When you pull something, it pinches. When you squeeze it, it bulges. This ratio quantifies that trade-off.

example.problem: A rod stretches by strain 0.01 and simultaneously compresses laterally by 0.003. Find Poisson's ratio.
example.solution: μ = 0.003 / 0.01 = 0.3 (typical for many metals).

slides.inSimpleWords: Poisson's ratio tells you: when the material stretches one way, how much does it shrink sideways?

image.alt: Poisson's Ratio: The Sideways Effect — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Example: Lateral Thinning Under Load
slides.storyContext: The steel rod stretches by 0.5 mm over 2 m length. Using Poisson's ratio μ = 0.3, how much does the diameter shrink?

example.problem: Rod diameter = 5 cm, length = 2 m, elongation = 0.5 mm, μ = 0.3. Find lateral contraction (diameter reduction).
example.solution: Longitudinal strain = 0.5 mm / 2000 mm = 0.00025. Lateral strain = μ × Longitudinal strain = 0.3 × 0.00025 = 0.000075. Diameter reduction = 50 mm × 0.000075 = 0.00375 mm ≈ 3.75 micrometers (tiny, but measurable!).

slides.inSimpleWords: As the rod stretches, it gets slightly thinner. Poisson's ratio quantifies this simultaneous deformation.

image.alt: Example: Lateral Thinning Under Load — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Practice Problem: Finding Required Diameter
slides.storyContext: Priya reverses the problem: if a rod must hold 8 kN with maximum elongation of 0.2 mm (over 2 m length), and steel E = 200 GPa, what diameter is needed?

example.problem: Load F = 8000 N, allowable elongation ΔL = 0.2 mm, length L = 2 m, E = 200 GPa. Find required diameter.
example.solution: Max strain = ΔL/L = 0.2/2000 = 0.0001. Max stress = E × strain = 200 × 10⁹ × 0.0001 = 2 × 10⁷ Pa = 20 MPa. Area needed A = F/stress = 8000 / (2 × 10⁷) = 4 × 10⁻⁴ m². For circular: πr² = 4 × 10⁻⁴, so r ≈ 0.0113 m = 11.3 mm. Diameter ≈ 22.6 mm or about 0.9 inches.

slides.inSimpleWords: Engineers design to limits, not just safety. Here, we found the minimum diameter that won't stretch more than 0.2 mm.

image.alt: Practice Problem: Finding Required Diameter — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Complete Bridge Calculation
slides.storyContext: Rajesh and Priya work through the full design check for a 2 cm-diameter steel rod supporting 5 kN (5,000 N).

example.problem: A steel rod (diameter 2 cm, original length 2 m, E = 200 GPa) supports a downward force of 5,000 N. (a) Calculate stress. (b) Calculate strain. (c) Calculate elongation. (d) Is it safe? (Breaking stress for steel ≈ 400 MPa.)
example.solution: (a) Cross-sectional area = π(0.01)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m². Stress = 5,000 / (3.14 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.59 × 10⁷ Pa = 15.9 MPa. (b) Strain = Stress / E = (1.59 × 10⁷) / (2 × 10¹¹) ≈ 7.95 × 10⁻⁵. (c) Elongation = Strain × Original length = (7.95 × 10⁻⁵) × 2 = 1.59 × 10⁻⁴ m ≈ 0.16 mm. (d) Yes, safe—15.9 MPa << 400 MPa breaking stress. The rod elongates by only 0.16 mm.

slides.inSimpleWords: By calculating stress and strain, engineers know the rod is safe and predict exactly how much it will stretch.

image.alt: Complete Bridge Calculation — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: The Aluminum Alternative
slides.storyContext: Gopal suggests using aluminum instead of steel to save cost. The aluminum rod also has diameter 2 cm and length 2 m. For aluminum: E ≈ 70 GPa, breaking stress ≈ 110 MPa. If the same 5 kN load is applied, how much will aluminum elongate? Is it safe?

example.problem: An aluminum rod (diameter 2 cm, length 2 m, E = 70 GPa, breaking stress = 110 MPa) supports 5,000 N. Calculate: (a) Stress (same as steel). (b) Strain. (c) Elongation. (d) Safety verdict.
example.solution: (a) Stress = 1.59 × 10⁷ Pa = 15.9 MPa (same area). (b) Strain = (1.59 × 10⁷) / (7 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 2.27 × 10⁻⁴. (c) Elongation = (2.27 × 10⁻⁴) × 2 ≈ 4.54 × 10⁻⁴ m ≈ 0.45 mm. (d) Safe, but stretches MORE than steel (0.45 mm vs. 0.16 mm) and the safety margin is lower. For a bridge carrying many people, steel is better.

image.alt: The Aluminum Alternative — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Challenge: Material Comparison Table
slides.storyContext: Rajesh creates a comparison of five common bridge-building materials. For each, given Young's modulus and breaking stress, calculate the maximum safe load (stress = 50% of breaking stress) and elongation for a 2 m rod with 2 cm diameter.

example.problem: Compare Steel (E = 200 GPa, σ_break = 400 MPa), Aluminum (E = 70 GPa, σ_break = 110 MPa), Titanium (E = 100 GPa, σ_break = 900 MPa) for same geometry. Find max safe load (50% safety factor).
example.solution: Steel: max stress = 200 MPa, max force = 200 × 10⁶ × 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ = 62.8 kN. Aluminum: max stress = 55 MPa, max force = 17.3 kN. Titanium: max stress = 450 MPa, max force = 141.3 kN. Titanium is strongest but expensive. Steel best balance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Engineers weigh cost vs. performance. Steel offers the best combination of strength and affordability for most bridges.

image.alt: Challenge: Material Comparison Table — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Practice: Multi-Step Design Problem
slides.storyContext: Final design check: A bridge cable must support 100 kN maximum with safety factor 4 and allow no more than 1 mm elongation over 10 m length.

example.problem: Find minimum diameter steel cable (E = 200 GPa, σ_break = 400 MPa). Constraints: (1) safe stress ≤ 400 MPa / 4 = 100 MPa, (2) strain ≤ 0.0001 (1 mm / 10 m).
example.solution: From constraint 1: A ≥ 100,000 / (100 × 10⁶) = 10⁻³ m² = 1000 mm². From constraint 2: stress ≤ E × strain = 200 × 10⁹ × 0.0001 = 20 MPa. This is MORE restrictive! A ≥ 100,000 / (20 × 10⁶) = 5 × 10⁻³ m² = 5000 mm². For circular πr² = 5000, r ≈ 39.9 mm, diameter ≈ 80 mm. Elongation limit, not strength, determines cable size!

slides.inSimpleWords: Real design problems have multiple constraints. Sometimes stiffness (elongation limit) is more restrictive than strength.

image.alt: Practice: Multi-Step Design Problem — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Practice: Heat Effects on Young's Modulus
slides.storyContext: Priya notes that materials soften at high temperatures. Steel E drops from 200 GPa at room temp to 180 GPa at 100°C. How does this affect the bridge on a hot day?

example.problem: Same 2 cm steel rod, 2 m long, 5 kN load. E drops from 200 GPa (cold) to 180 GPa (hot). Find elongation at each temperature.
example.solution: Stress = 1.59 × 10⁷ Pa (same). At 200 GPa: strain = 1.59 × 10⁷ / 2 × 10¹¹ = 7.95 × 10⁻⁵, elongation = 0.159 mm. At 180 GPa: strain = 1.59 × 10⁷ / 1.8 × 10¹¹ = 8.83 × 10⁻⁵, elongation = 0.177 mm. That's 0.018 mm more stretch—small but noticeable!

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature matters. Hot materials are softer and stretch more than cold ones. Bridge designers account for this.

image.alt: Practice: Heat Effects on Young's Modulus — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Real-World Bridge Inspection
slides.storyContext: Rajesh and Priya visit an old bridge to inspect for fatigue cracks. 'Over decades, small stress cycles damage the metal. Even below breaking stress, material fails from repeated loading.' This is why engineers apply safety factors.

image.alt: Real-World Bridge Inspection — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Malleability vs. Brittleness
slides.storyContext: At the materials lab, Priya and Rajesh observe two test results: steel deforms significantly before breaking (plastic deformation), while cast iron breaks suddenly with little warning. 'Which is safer for a bridge?' asks Rajesh. 'Definitely steel,' says Priya. 'You see deformation coming. Cast iron just snaps.'

image.alt: Malleability vs. Brittleness — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Elastic vs. Plastic Deformation
slides.storyContext: Priya explains the two regions on a stress-strain curve: 'Below the yield point, the material springs back (elastic). Beyond it, the material stays deformed permanently (plastic).'

points.label: Elastic region
points.text: Below yield stress: material returns to original shape when load is removed. Follows Hooke's Law: Stress ∝ Strain.

points.label: Plastic region
points.text: Above yield stress: material stays permanently deformed even after load is removed. Occurs before material breaks.

points.label: Ductility
points.text: Ductile materials (steel) show large plastic region before breaking. Brittle materials (cast iron, glass) show minimal plastic region.

points.label: Engineer's advantage
points.text: Ductile materials give warning (visible deformation) before failure. Brittle materials fail suddenly with no warning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Steel stretches visibly before breaking—engineers see trouble coming. Cast iron snaps suddenly—dangerous in structures.

image.alt: Elastic vs. Plastic Deformation — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Example: Yield Point Identification
slides.storyContext: Priya plots stress vs. strain for steel. 'The yield point is where the curve stops being linear. Below, Hooke's Law works perfectly. Above, the material yields.'

example.problem: A steel sample yields at stress 250 MPa and breaks at 400 MPa. If we apply 300 MPa stress and then release it, the sample has permanent elongation of 0.05%. Was it in the elastic or plastic region?
example.solution: 300 MPa > 250 MPa (yield point), so it entered the plastic region. After removing the load, 0.05% permanent strain remains—confirming plastic (permanent) deformation occurred.

slides.inSimpleWords: The yield point marks the transition from elastic (reversible) to plastic (permanent) deformation. It's the limit of safe stress.

image.alt: Example: Yield Point Identification — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: Challenge: Safety Factor Design
slides.storyContext: A cable must safely support 5 tons (50 kN) on the bridge. Steel cable (E = 200 GPa, breaking stress = 400 MPa) is available. Using a safety factor of 5, what diameter cable is needed?

example.problem: Required safe stress = Breaking stress / Safety factor = 400 MPa / 5 = 80 MPa. Required stress area A = Force / Stress = (50 × 10³ N) / (80 × 10⁶ Pa) = 6.25 × 10⁻⁴ m². For circular cross-section: πr² = 6.25 × 10⁻⁴, so r = √(6.25 × 10⁻⁴ / π) ≈ 0.0141 m ≈ 14.1 mm. Diameter ≈ 28.2 mm ≈ 1.1 inches.
example.solution: A steel cable just over 1 inch diameter can safely support 5 tons with 5× safety margin. If loads vary, engineers might choose 1.25 inch (32 mm) for extra security.

slides.inSimpleWords: Safety factors account for unexpected stresses, material defects, and fatigue. Engineers always build in generous margins.

image.alt: Challenge: Safety Factor Design — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: The Bridge Opens
slides.storyContext: Six months later, the bridge is complete and safe for traffic. Rajesh, Priya, and Gopal watch villagers crossing. 'All of this physics made this possible,' says Priya. 'Understanding materials saved lives.'

image.alt: The Bridge Opens — Mechanical Properties of Solids

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: Rajesh chose steel for the bridge. Here's why, in bullet points:

points.text: Stress = Force / Area; Strain = Change / Original dimension.
Young's modulus E = Stress / Strain; higher E = stiffer material.
Every material has an elastic limit (reversible deformation) and a breaking stress (fracture point).
Steel is stiffer and stronger than aluminum; it stretches less under the same load and has a higher safety margin for a footbridge.
Poisson's ratio describes lateral contraction when material is stretched—materials thin slightly as they lengthen.
Engineers use these calculations to predict real behavior, choose the right material for safety, and apply safety factors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understand stress and strain, know the Young's modulus of your material, check that applied stress is well below breaking stress, and you can build something that lasts.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Mechanical Properties of Solids

subject: Physics
title: The Village Water System Mystery
hook: Why does water flow faster from the bottom tap than the top, and why is oil thicker than water?

slides.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
slides.storyContext: The village has built a water tank 10 meters high. But why does water spray out stronger from the bottom tap? And why does the molasses at the temple flow so slowly compared to water? Vikram the physics teacher explains.

image.alt: Mechanical Properties of Fluids — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: The Pressure Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Rohan watches water flow from three taps on the tank—top, middle, and bottom. 'Sir, the bottom one shoots the farthest! Does pressure change with depth?' Vikram smiles. 'Exactly. Let's measure it.'

image.alt: The Pressure Puzzle — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: The Viscosity Discovery
slides.storyContext: Anjali pours water and honey side by side onto a slanted board. Water rushes down. Honey oozes slowly. 'Why such different speeds?' asks Rohan. 'That's viscosity,' Vikram says. 'It measures how much the liquid resists flowing—how much friction is inside the liquid itself.'

image.alt: The Viscosity Discovery — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Pressure in Fluids at Rest
slides.storyContext: Vikram fills a tall container and pokes holes at different heights. Water sprays farthest from the bottom hole.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Pressure P = Force / Area (unit: Pa). In fluids: P = ρgh, where ρ = density, g = 9.8 m/s², h = depth.

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Pressure increases linearly with depth because of the weight of fluid above.

example.problem: The water tank is 10 m deep. What is the pressure at the bottom? (ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)

slides.inSimpleWords: The deeper you go in water, the more weight presses down on you. That creates pressure, which is why the bottom tap shoots harder.

image.alt: Pressure in Fluids at Rest — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Example: Pressure at Different Depths
slides.storyContext: Calculate the water pressure at the top, middle, and bottom of the village tank (10 m total height).

example.problem: Water tank height = 10 m. Find pressure at (a) top (h = 0), (b) middle (h = 5 m), (c) bottom (h = 10 m). ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s².
example.solution: (a) P_top = 1000 × 9.8 × 0 = 0 Pa (reference point). (b) P_middle = 1000 × 9.8 × 5 = 49,000 Pa = 49 kPa. (c) P_bottom = 1000 × 9.8 × 10 = 98,000 Pa = 98 kPa. Pressure doubles as you go from middle to bottom!

slides.inSimpleWords: Pressure increases linearly with depth. The bottom of the tank experiences twice the pressure of the midpoint.

image.alt: Example: Pressure at Different Depths — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Viscosity: How Thick Is the Liquid?
slides.storyContext: Rohan pours water and oil side by side. 'Water flows like it's in a hurry. Oil moves like molasses in winter.' Vikram explains friction inside liquids.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Viscosity η = resistance to flow. Unit: Pa·s (Pascal-second). Stokes (St) = 10⁻⁴ Pa·s.

points.label: Real values
points.text: Water: ~0.001 Pa·s at 20°C. Oil: ~0.1 Pa·s. Honey: ~10 Pa·s. Syrup: ~1 Pa·s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Viscosity is how thick or sticky a liquid feels. Higher viscosity = flows slower. Water is slippery (low η), honey is gooey (high η).

image.alt: Viscosity: How Thick Is the Liquid? — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Example: Viscosity Comparison
slides.storyContext: Vikram drips equal volumes of different liquids and times how long each takes to fall 10 cm. Let's calculate their relative viscosities.

example.problem: Water takes 1 second to fall 10 cm. Oil takes 10 seconds for the same distance. Honey takes 100 seconds. Compare their viscosities assuming the time ratio equals the viscosity ratio.
example.solution: Water: η_w ≈ 0.001 Pa·s (ref). Oil: η_o ≈ 10 × 0.001 = 0.01 Pa·s (10× thicker). Honey: η_h ≈ 100 × 0.001 = 0.1 Pa·s (100× thicker). In reality, water is 0.001, oil is ~0.1, honey is ~10 Pa·s, so the trend holds!

slides.inSimpleWords: Thicker liquids flow slower. The more viscous the liquid, the longer it takes to fall or pour.

image.alt: Example: Viscosity Comparison — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Stokes' Law: When a Ball Falls Through Fluid
slides.storyContext: Rohan drops a marble into water, then into oil. The marble sinks fast in water, but crawls through oil. Why?

points.label: Stokes' Law
points.text: The drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid: F_drag = 6πηrv, where η = viscosity, r = radius, v = velocity.

points.label: Terminal velocity
points.text: When drag force equals weight, the sphere stops accelerating and falls at constant speed (terminal velocity).

example.problem: A steel ball (radius 1 cm, mass 10 g) falls through oil (η = 0.1 Pa·s). At terminal velocity, drag force = weight. Calculate terminal velocity if weight = 0.1 N.
example.solution: At terminal velocity: 6πηrv = mg. So v = mg / (6πηr) = 0.1 / (6π × 0.1 × 0.01) ≈ 0.1 / 0.0188 ≈ 5.3 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: A falling object in a thick liquid reaches a maximum speed (terminal velocity) when drag friction equals its weight.

image.alt: Stokes' Law: When a Ball Falls Through Fluid — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Example: Terminal Velocity in Water vs. Oil
slides.storyContext: Compare how fast the marble falls in water (η = 0.001 Pa·s) versus oil (η = 0.1 Pa·s).

example.problem: Same marble, radius r = 1 cm, weight = 0.1 N. Terminal velocity v = mg / (6πηr). Find v_water and v_oil.
example.solution: v_water = 0.1 / (6π × 0.001 × 0.01) = 0.1 / 0.000188 ≈ 531 m/s (impossible; actually limited by drag at lower speeds). v_oil = 0.1 / (6π × 0.1 × 0.01) = 0.1 / 0.0188 ≈ 5.3 m/s. Oil viscosity is 100× higher, so terminal velocity is 100× lower! The marble crawls through oil.

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher viscosity drastically slows falling objects. Oil is 100 times more viscous than water, so objects fall 100 times slower.

image.alt: Example: Terminal Velocity in Water vs. Oil — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Pascal's Principle: Pressure Transmits Equally
slides.storyContext: Anjali uses a hydraulic pump to lift a heavy motorcycle at the garage. She barely pushes, yet it rises. 'How does that work?'

points.label: Pascal's Principle
points.text: Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.

points.label: Hydraulic advantage
points.text: Force_out / Force_in = Area_out / Area_in. A small force on a small piston multiplies into a large force on a large piston.

example.problem: A hydraulic jack has a small piston (area 10 cm²) and large piston (area 1000 cm²). If Anjali pushes with 500 N, what weight can the large piston lift?
example.solution: Force_out = Force_in × (Area_out / Area_in) = 500 × (1000 / 10) = 500 × 100 = 50,000 N. The jack lifts a 5-ton motorcycle!

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydraulic systems use Pascal's principle: apply a small force on a small area to generate a huge force on a large area—no magic, just pressure.

image.alt: Pascal's Principle: Pressure Transmits Equally — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Continuity Equation: How Much Flows Through?
slides.storyContext: Water flows from the tank through pipes of different widths. 'When the pipe narrows, the water speeds up,' Rohan observes.

points.label: Continuity Equation
points.text: For incompressible flow: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, where A = cross-sectional area, v = velocity.

points.label: Physical meaning
points.text: The volume flow rate (volume per second) stays constant. Narrow pipe = fast flow; wide pipe = slow flow.

example.problem: Water flows through a pipe. At point 1 (diameter 4 cm), velocity is 2 m/s. At point 2 (diameter 2 cm), what is the velocity?

slides.inSimpleWords: Water must flow the same total amount through every part of a pipe. A narrower section forces the water to move faster.

image.alt: Continuity Equation: How Much Flows Through? — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Example: Flow Rate in Village Pipeline
slides.storyContext: The main pipe from the tank (diameter 10 cm) carries water to the village. If water moves at 1.5 m/s here, what is the volume flow rate?

example.problem: Main pipe diameter D = 10 cm = 0.1 m, velocity v = 1.5 m/s. Calculate volume flow rate Q = Av.
example.solution: Area A = π(0.05)² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m². Flow rate Q = A × v = (7.85 × 10⁻³) × 1.5 = 0.01177 m³/s ≈ 11.8 L/s. This supplies multiple villages!

slides.inSimpleWords: Volume flow rate tells us how many liters per second flow through a pipe—crucial for water supply planning.

image.alt: Example: Flow Rate in Village Pipeline — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Practice: Pressure Drop in Narrowing Pipe
slides.storyContext: Water flows from a 4 cm diameter section into a 2 cm diameter section. Using Bernoulli's equation and continuity, find the pressure change if inlet pressure is 200 kPa and velocity is 1 m/s.

example.problem: Section 1: D₁ = 4 cm, P₁ = 200 kPa, v₁ = 1 m/s. Section 2: D₂ = 2 cm. Find v₂ and P₂.
example.solution: From continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. (π × 0.02² × 1) = (π × 0.01² × v₂), so v₂ = 4 m/s. From Bernoulli: P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂². P₂ = 200,000 + ½ × 1000 × (1 - 16) = 200,000 - 7,500 = 192.5 kPa. Pressure drops by 7.5 kPa as velocity quadruples!

slides.inSimpleWords: Narrowing pipes speed up water and drop pressure simultaneously—a fundamental principle in fluid dynamics.

image.alt: Practice: Pressure Drop in Narrowing Pipe — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Bernoulli's Principle: The Fast Flow Paradox
slides.storyContext: Vikram holds two papers upright, close together. He blows between them. 'They move closer, not apart! Why?'

points.label: Bernoulli's Principle
points.text: For flowing fluid: P + (1/2)ρv² + ρgh = constant. Where fast flow occurs, pressure is LOW.

points.label: The paradox
points.text: Higher velocity means lower pressure—so fast air between the papers pulls them together, not pushes apart.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a fluid flows fast, its pressure drops. This is why airplane wings create lift and why fast-moving water has lower pressure than still water.

image.alt: Bernoulli's Principle: The Fast Flow Paradox — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Example: Bernoulli's Equation Applied
slides.storyContext: Water exits a pipe narrowing (1 inch to 0.5 inch diameter). Using Bernoulli's equation, relate velocity and pressure changes.

example.problem: Wide section: area A₁ = 5 cm², velocity v₁ = 2 m/s, pressure P₁ = 100 kPa. Narrow section: area A₂ = 1.25 cm². Find v₂ and P₂ using continuity and Bernoulli.
example.solution: From continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → v₂ = (5 × 2) / 1.25 = 8 m/s. From Bernoulli (assuming same height): P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂². So P₂ = P₁ + ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = 100,000 + ½ × 1000 × (4 − 64) = 100,000 − 30,000 = 70 kPa. Pressure drops by 30 kPa as velocity quadruples!

slides.inSimpleWords: When water speeds up in a narrower pipe, its pressure drops significantly. Fast flow means low pressure.

image.alt: Example: Bernoulli's Equation Applied — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Complete Flow Problem: The Village Pipeline
slides.storyContext: Water flows from the tank (depth 10 m) through a pipe of diameter 5 cm. What is the pressure at the tank bottom, and at what speed will water flow out?

example.problem: A cylindrical tank (10 m deep, filled with water) has a drain valve at the bottom with area 5 cm². (a) Calculate pressure at tank bottom. (b) Assuming Bernoulli's principle (no friction), at what speed does water exit the drain? (c) What is the volume flow rate? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)
example.solution: (a) P = ρgh = 1000 × 9.8 × 10 = 98,000 Pa. (b) From Bernoulli: P + (1/2)ρv² = P_atm + 0 (at surface, v ≈ 0). So (1/2)ρv² = ρgh, giving v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 10) = √196 ≈ 14 m/s. (c) Q = Av = (5 × 10⁻³) × 14 = 0.07 m³/s = 70 L/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Using pressure, Bernoulli's principle, and continuity, we can predict exactly how fast and how much water flows from any tap on a tank.

image.alt: Complete Flow Problem: The Village Pipeline — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: The Oil vs. Water Race
slides.storyContext: Two identical containers—one filled with water, one with oil—are drained through identical holes at the bottom at the same time. Oil takes much longer to empty. Using Stokes' Law and viscosity, explain why the oil drains slower than water, and estimate the time ratio.

example.problem: Water (η ≈ 0.001 Pa·s) and oil (η ≈ 0.1 Pa·s) drain from identical containers. Assume internal friction dominates (high viscosity effects). The time to drain is inversely proportional to the speed of flow, which depends on viscosity. If water takes 10 seconds, how long will oil take? (Assume the proportionality t ∝ η.)
example.solution: Since flow rate is inversely related to viscosity: t_oil / t_water = η_oil / η_water = 0.1 / 0.001 = 100. Oil takes 100 × 10 seconds = 1000 seconds ≈ 16.7 minutes, while water drains in 10 seconds!

image.alt: The Oil vs. Water Race — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Challenge: Hydraulic Lift Design
slides.storyContext: Anjali wants to design a hydraulic lift for her farm equipment (mass 500 kg). If she can apply 400 N force on the input piston, what should be the area ratio (large to small) for the lift to work?

example.problem: Desired output force = weight of 500 kg = 5000 N. Input force = 400 N. Find the required area ratio A_out / A_in from F_out / F_in = A_out / A_in.
example.solution: Area ratio = F_out / F_in = 5000 / 400 = 12.5. If small piston has area 10 cm², large piston must have area 125 cm². This is achievable and practical!

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydraulic systems trade distance for force. Push a small piston far to lift a large mass a short distance.

image.alt: Challenge: Hydraulic Lift Design — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Practice: Combining Pressure, Flow, and Viscosity
slides.storyContext: A water pump must lift 50 liters/minute from 5 m depth and deliver through 50 m of horizontal pipe (diameter 2 cm).

example.problem: Calculate: (1) pressure to lift water 5 m, (2) additional pressure for friction in 50 m horizontal pipe, (3) total pump power needed.
example.solution: (1) P_static = ρgh = 1000 × 9.8 × 5 = 49 kPa. (2) For flow Q = 50 L/min = 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s, velocity v = Q/A = 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ / (π × 0.01²) ≈ 2.65 m/s. Friction loss (using Darcy): P_friction ≈ 0.02 × (L/D) × (ρv²/2) ≈ 0.02 × (50/0.02) × (1000 × 2.65²/2) ≈ 70 kPa. (3) Total pressure ≈ 119 kPa. Power = P × Q = 119,000 × 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 99 W ≈ 0.13 horsepower.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pump design requires balancing static pressure (lifting), dynamic pressure (friction), and flow rate for optimal efficiency.

image.alt: Practice: Combining Pressure, Flow, and Viscosity — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Practice: Reynolds Number and Flow Regimes
slides.storyContext: Vikram introduces the Reynolds number Re = ρvD/η, which predicts whether flow is smooth (laminar) or chaotic (turbulent).

example.problem: Water flows through a 5 cm pipe at 2 m/s. ρ = 1000 kg/m³, η = 0.001 Pa·s. Calculate Reynolds number. Re < 2300 is laminar, Re > 4000 is turbulent.
example.solution: Re = (1000 × 2 × 0.05) / 0.001 = 100 / 0.001 = 100,000. Highly turbulent! The flow is chaotic with eddies and mixing. Higher viscosity or lower velocity would give laminar flow.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reynolds number predicts flow behavior. Low Re means smooth laminar flow; high Re means chaotic turbulent flow.

slides.storyContext: Vikram shows Rohan two pipes: one with smooth laminar flow (quiet), the other turbulent and churning (noisy). 'Turbulence wastes energy as heat and sound. That's why pipes need to balance flow rate and pressure drop.'

slides.title: Surface Tension and Capillary Action
slides.storyContext: Rohan notices water clinging to plant roots in the garden, rising against gravity. 'How does water climb up?' Vikram smiles: 'Surface tension and adhesion—molecules at the surface stick together, pulling water upward in tiny pores.'

image.alt: Surface Tension and Capillary Action — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

slides.title: Surface Tension and Interfacial Phenomena
slides.storyContext: Vikram drips water onto a leaf and it beads up into a sphere. 'That's surface tension—the liquid surface acts like a stretched rubber skin.'

points.label: Surface tension γ
points.text: The energy (or force) per unit length at the liquid-air interface. Unit: N/m. Water: ~0.072 N/m at 20°C.

points.label: Capillary rise
points.text: h = 2γ cos(θ) / (ρgr), where θ = contact angle, r = tube radius. Narrow tubes show larger capillary rise.

points.label: Meniscus
points.text: Curved surface of liquid in a tube due to adhesion (liquid wets tube) vs. cohesion (liquid molecules attract each other).

points.label: Real applications
points.text: Plant roots absorb water by capillary action. Wicking in paper towels. Detergents reduce surface tension to help water wet fabric.

slides.inSimpleWords: Surface tension is why water beads up and why plants can drink water against gravity. It's a cohesive force at molecular boundaries.

slides.title: Challenge: Siphon Flow Analysis
slides.storyContext: Rohan sets up a siphon to drain water from a high tank to a lower basin. If the difference in height is 2 m and he uses a 2 cm diameter hose, how long will it take to transfer 100 liters?

example.problem: Height difference h = 2 m. Exit velocity from Bernoulli: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 2) ≈ 6.26 m/s. Pipe diameter = 2 cm, so area A = π(0.01)² ≈ 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m². Flow rate Q = Av = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ × 6.26 ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻³ m³/s ≈ 2 L/s. Time to transfer 100 L = 100 / 2 = 50 seconds.
example.solution: The siphon drains 100 liters in about 50 seconds. This is much faster than if water flowed under normal pressure, showing the power of hydrostatic pressure!

slides.inSimpleWords: A siphon uses the difference in height to create flow without a pump. Physics does the work for free!

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The village water system now makes perfect sense. Here's the summary:

points.text: Pressure in a fluid at rest increases with depth: P = ρgh. Deeper = stronger spray.
Viscosity η measures resistance to flow. Water flows fast (low η); oil flows slow (high η).
Stokes' Law: drag force F = 6πηrv; objects reach terminal velocity when drag equals weight.
Pascal's Principle: pressure transmits equally in confined fluids—basis of hydraulic systems.
Continuity Equation: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Narrow pipe = fast flow; wide pipe = slow flow.
Bernoulli's Principle: fast flow = low pressure. Used in airplane wings, venturi tubes, and understanding jets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fluids follow predictable laws. Pressure, viscosity, and flow rate determine how water moves from your tap, how engines work, and why planes can fly.
